The crossing took nineteen minutes. She had made it, by her own careless count, some twenty thousand times, and she had stopped counting because the number had begun to feel less like a record and more like a debt.

A man came down the ramp at the last sailing with a coat too thin for the water and nothing in his hands. He stood at the rail instead of taking a seat, which told her most of what she needed to know.

"Is this the boat for the island?"

"It's the only boat."

"I meant—does anyone come back on it?"

Mireille loosed the stern line and let the engine catch. She had learned that people asked whether anyone came back when they meant to, and asked whether it was the only boat when they had already decided not to.

"Same boat," she said. "Different people."

He smiled without much in it and gripped the rail. Midway across, the wind came down the channel and the deck began its slow roll, the way it always did. He shifted his feet.

"Does it always do that?"

"Every crossing. Same stretch."

"Then you'd think you'd stop noticing."

"You'd think." She eased the throttle. "But I want to notice. The day the water feels ordinary is the day I stop watching it."

The island lights came up, small and steady. He didn't move toward the bow.

"Last return's at ten," she said. "You don't have to decide yet."

"When do I have to?"

"At ten," said Mireille. "That's what the schedule is for.""}
